blocks.text: *Toý* means a feast, a celebration, and above all a wedding. For a Turkmen family a wedding is one of the great events of life, and it brings the whole family together, from the grandparents to the youngest *jigi*, with the *daýy*, *daýza* and *bibi* of this unit and many neighbours. Turkmenportal, a news and culture site in Ashgabat, writes that 200 to 300 guests are usual, and that a thousand is not unheard of.

The celebrations traditionally last about three days, with customs at the bride's home and at the groom's, and they are prepared for months. Today the main evening often takes place in a restaurant or a banquet hall; in Ashgabat, many weddings are held at *Bagt köşgi*, the Palace of Happiness. There is plenty of food, loud music, and dancing all evening.

The bride, *gelin*, traditionally wears a red dress of fine silk under a richly embroidered robe, covered in silver jewellery. A scarlet embroidered robe, the *kürte*, is placed over her head; covering the bride was long thought to protect her from evil. The full costume can be very heavy: Turkmenportal says the dress with its ornaments can weigh over 25 kg. Many couples also change into a white dress and a dark suit for part of the evening.

The silver is part of an old art. Turkmen women's jewellery, often set with red carnelian, was sewn onto clothes and worn on the head, the neck and the hands. At the wedding the girl's headdress was replaced by a married woman's, decorated with silver, as a museum story on Google Arts and Culture describes.

Music carries the feast. One tradition is *küştdepdi*, a rite of song and dance in which singers improvise verses of good wishes and dancers move with the rhythm, hands and feet together. It belongs to family events such as births and weddings and to public celebrations, and UNESCO added it to its list of the intangible heritage of humanity in 2017. Dancing guests often hand out small gifts, such as scarves or sweets.

blocks.title: Words for the day
blocks.text: *gelin* is the bride, and also a daughter-in-law; *giýew* is the groom, and a son-in-law. A woman *durmuşa çykýar* (gets married), a man *öýlenýär*. To congratulate, say *Gutly bolsun!*
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Ertir toý bar: uýam durmuşa çykýar! Öýümizde myhman köp. Ejäm we kakam bagtly. Atam we enäm hem gelýärler.
blocks.en: Tomorrow there's a wedding: my older sister is getting married! There are lots of guests in our house. My mum and dad are happy. My grandfather and grandmother are coming too.
